blocks.text: Mutations that change only one or a few nucleotides are point mutations.

items: Substitution: one nucleotide is exchanged for another, for example A replaced by G or C by T during replication.
Insertion: one or more extra nucleotides are added, usually by errors in replication.
Deletion: one or more nucleotides are removed.

blocks.title: For information: gene mutation
blocks.text: Gene mutation is a general term for any change within the chemical structure of a single gene: a change at the molecular (nucleotide) level rather than the chromosomal level. Point mutations are the most common gene mutations.

items: Ionizing radiation: X-rays and gamma rays are highly mutagenic; they change atoms into free radicals that can break the phosphodiester bonds of a DNA strand.
Ultraviolet radiation: DNA absorbs UV strongly; when two adjacent pyrimidines (C and T) absorb it, covalent bonds form between them, which can block replication completely.

Mutagenic chemicals: some resemble nucleotides and are built into DNA, which then cannot be transcribed properly; some remove the amino group from adenine or cytosine, and some add hydrocarbon groups to nucleotides, both causing mis-pairing. Such chemicals are used in laboratories and are sometimes released into the environment, for example mustard gas.

Spontaneous mutations: a nucleotide may shift to an alternative form so that DNA polymerase pairs the wrong partner with it; or sequences misalign when homologous chromosomes pair, a loop forms and is cut out, deleting several hundred nucleotides from one chromosome.

blocks.title: Why are most mutations harmful?
blocks.text: Most mutations disrupt the normal working of genes. A change of a single amino acid in haemoglobin can cause sickle cell anaemia; mutations that disrupt gene regulation can alter development and contribute to diseases such as cancer; and some give non-functional or unstable proteins, as in phenylketonuria.
Single-gene disorders can be inherited in an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive or X-linked way. Two important examples follow.

It is due to a recessive allele for an abnormal beta chain of haemoglobin, on chromosome 11. In the mutant allele the DNA nucleotide T is replaced by A, so the triplet CTC for glutamic acid becomes CAC, for valine. A child with two mutant alleles makes abnormal beta chains: the haemoglobin carries less oxygen and the red cells become sickle-shaped. Symptoms include pain, fatigue, shortness of breath, jaundice and more infections.

blocks.alt: Left: normal DNA, coding GAG over template CTC; a nucleotide substitution gives GTG over CAC. Transcription gives the mRNA codons GAG and GUG; translation gives glutamic acid and valine in the chain of amino acids; these lead to a normal round red blood cell and a sickle-shaped red blood cell.

blocks.text: Treatment includes pain relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and opioids; blood transfusions to raise the number of healthy red cells; bone marrow transplants, which can give a long-term cure; and regular monitoring with vaccinations and antibiotics to prevent complications.

A normal gene on chromosome 12 makes the liver enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), which converts the amino acid phenylalanine into tyrosine. A point mutation, such as a substitution or deletion, gives a recessive allele; a child with two recessive alleles makes too little working PAH, and phenylalanine builds up to toxic levels in the blood and tissues. Symptoms include intellectual disability, seizures, behavioural problems, mental disorder, microcephaly (a small head) and a musty odour of breath, skin and urine; excess phenylalanine can damage the brain.

People with PKU avoid foods high in phenylalanine, such as meat, dairy products, eggs and some grains, and their blood levels are checked regularly to adjust the diet. Some medicines contain synthetic PAH enzyme to lower blood phenylalanine; supplements supply vitamins and minerals that a low-phenylalanine diet may lack.

blocks.title: Possible ways to treat genetic diseases
blocks.text: Gene therapy corrects or replaces a mutated gene with a working one. Cell therapy replaces faulty cells with healthy ones, for example insulin-making beta cells in type 1 diabetes. Pharmacogenomics chooses the best drug from a patient's DNA. Genetic counselling gives families with a history of genetic disease testing, education and guidance on family planning.
